facts.value: Welsh Government has offered councils a new flexibility to take a full or part MRP payment holiday for 2026-27, with repayment over up to ten years. Pembrokeshire has included the discretion in its 2026-27 MRP policy to allow the Director of Resources to use it if needed 'e.g. to mitigate an unforeseen financial pressure in 2026-27' — while stating there are no plans to utilise it to bridge the projected funding gap and balance the 2026-27 budget, AND that 'it is difficult to see how this new flexibility complies with the Wellbeing of Future Generations Act'

source.title: Treasury Management Governance Arrangements — Council, 20 February 2026 (cover, doc 82945)

facts.note: Distinctive framing. The discretion-plus-reservation combination — take the option in case it's needed AND publicly flag WFG Act non-compliance concerns — is unusual across the library. The paper is careful to separate contingency from intention. This is the email's lead hook.

facts.value: External borrowing forecast to rise to £391.9m by 2029-30, an increase of £199.9m from 2024-25 for the current and approved capital programme. Implied 2024-25 external borrowing £192.0m — external debt more than doubles in five years

source.title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy 2026-27 to 2029-30 — Council, 20 February 2026 (doc 82999)

facts.note: The only explicit external-borrowing figure in either paper for this meeting. No CFR is disclosed alongside it, so the balance-sheet identity cannot be run.

facts.value: General Fund ratio: 3.38% (2025-26 est), 3.92% (2026-27), 4.15% (2027-28), 4.13% (2028-29), 4.01% (2029-30) — Approved Capital Programme. Cap set at 5.30% (Council decision 14 December 2023). Capacity under the cap: 1.92% / 1.38% / 1.15% / 1.17% / 1.29%. Variance vs 2025-26 budget: saving of £1,535k in 26-27; then annual revenue pressures of £1,288k / £458k / £78k

source.title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy — Table 1 p.29, methodology p.17

facts.note: HRA ratio not printed — only General Fund. The cap methodology replaced the older prudential-indicator framing at Pembrokeshire in December 2023.

facts.value: Modelling of an additional £149m borrowing profiled to 2041-42 keeps the GF ratio under the 5.30% cap. Outer-year peak 5.29% in 2041-42 — one basis point below the cap. Committed £19.3m of the £149m (Milford Haven Schools). Remaining capacity £129.7m. Cumulative annual revenue pressure builds to £11,890k by 2041-42

source.title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy — Table 2 p.31

facts.note: Ratio profile within the £149m model: 4.03% (26-27) rising through 4.75%, 4.84%, 5.05%, 5.11%, 5.04%, 5.25%, 5.24%, 5.25% ... 5.29% by 2041-42. Peak sits directly under the cap. Not a compliance issue — a modelled choice to use available capacity fully — but noted.

facts.value: £299m of additional borrowing required for schemes on the horizon over the period to 2041-42 (Table 3 total £846.344m of capital cost, of which £298.745m is PCC — council share). This is £169m MORE than the £129.7m capacity Table 2 leaves under the cap. Paper acknowledges the gap openly: 'accelerating/pausing schemes may be required to match the capital financing budget available to fund the borrowing'

source.title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy — Table 3 p.33, narrative p.32

facts.note: The paper prints the constraint before the constraint binds. Structural transparency of the same shape (though driven by a different reason) as Warwickshire — worth flagging into the library of 'councils that print the constraint before it binds'. Not raised as a criticism in the email; the reasoning is the council's own.

facts.value: Capital programme 2025-26 to 2029-30: £157.3m / £192.0m / £105.1m / £99.8m / £92.8m. Loan financing component: £47.4m / £84.8m / £56.1m / £47.7m / £35.8m — peaks at £84.8m in 2026-27 (year strategy is set), more than double 2025-26. HRA Borrowing Cap component: £16.7m / £36.7m / £28.1m / £23.4m / £10.3m — also peaks in 2026-27 at £36.7m

source.title: Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy — Table 4 p.37

facts.note: The strategy explicitly flags that the capital programme has not been updated to reflect the proposed HRA capital investment being presented to Cabinet on 16 March 2026 (Appendix p.36). So a further HRA revision is pipelined.

facts.value: Implicit internal-borrowing / short-term stance disclosed in the slippage narrative: 'Reduced capital spend has resulted in a reduced need to borrow which has benefited the Council when borrowing rates have remained high and the Council has been able to utilise their cashflow along with short-term borrowing to manage cashflow fluctuations and to limit expensive long-term debt' (Appendix p.28). Rule of thumb: £60k revenue pressure per £1m borrowed, at an assumed 4.0% (Appendix p.4)
facts.note: No CFR/liability benchmark/external-borrowing spot figure printed anywhere in these two papers, so the internal-borrowing size cannot be quantified from what is held. The stance is disclosed, not quantified.

summary.text:
Pembrokeshire's Council on 20 February 2026 approved the Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 to 2029-30. The paper on disk is the three-page cover report (doc 82945) plus the 51-page Appendix H(i) Capital Strategy 2026-27 to 2029-30 (doc 82999). The full TMSS annex referenced in the cover — 'Annual Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy' — is NOT among the papers listed for this meeting on disk. Consequently no CFR, no external-borrowing spot figure at year-end, no maturity profile, no operational boundary, no authorised limit, no liability benchmark and no loan-book table are held from this meeting. The balance-sheet identity therefore cannot be run.

What the two papers held do carry is a set of things most council TMSSs / Capital Strategies do not: the cover paper folds the Welsh Government MRP payment-holiday flexibility into the 2026-27 MRP policy to give the S151 discretion, and in the same paragraph publishes the reservation 'it is difficult to see how this new flexibility complies with the Wellbeing of Future Generations Act'. It also states outright that there are no plans to use it to bridge the projected funding gap. Discretion-as-contingency plus a published reservation is unusual; that is the email's lead hook.

The prudential-discipline material sits alongside. Council approved a Capital Financing Costs to Net Revenue Budget cap of 5.30% for the General Fund in December 2023. Table 1 on page 29 has the approved programme running 3.38% (25-26) / 3.92% (26-27) / 4.15% / 4.13% / 4.01%, with 1.15%-1.38% capacity from 2026-27 through 2029-30 (year-by-year variance vs 2025-26 budget: −£1,535k / +£1,288k / +£458k / +£78k). Table 2 on page 31 then models the additional £149m borrowing profiled to 2041-42 within the cap — outer-year ratio 5.29%, one basis point below the 5.30%. Table 3 discloses £299m of schemes on the horizon to 2041-42, £169m more than the £129.7m capacity Table 2 leaves. Printing the cap, the trajectory, the peak against the cap, and the gap between schemes-needed and capacity-available, in the same document, is unusual — most papers print one of those, not all four.

Table 4 on page 37 has the approved capital programme running £157.3m / £192.0m / £105.1m / £99.8m / £92.8m, of which loan financing is £47.4m / £84.8m / £56.1m / £47.7m / £35.8m — peaking at £84.8m in 2026-27, more than double 2025-26. HRA borrowing peaks at £36.7m in 2026-27. And page 15 discloses that external borrowing is forecast to rise to £391.9m by 2029-30, up £199.9m (i.e. more than double) from £192m in 2024-25.

Loan-book reconciliation cannot be performed. The paper carries no PWLB total or weighted rate. Our file for PEMBROKESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL (borrower name verified via price_book.py --find) at 2026-03-31 has 57 loans, £170,193,660 principal, weighted 4.4505% — recorded internally only. Per PIPELINE.md the loan-book claim is kept out of the email entirely. The break-cost engine returns a net indicative discount of £14.87m (8.9% of principal) concentrated in four low-coupon long-dated MATURITY loans (1.68% to 2.25% coupons, maturities 2063-2069) — a substantive follow-up conversation on its own terms, but also kept out of the email until the underlying loan-file totals can be tied to a paper.

The email is built on three treasury-side observations that need no loan-book anchor: the MRP payment-holiday framing (lead), the prudential-discipline transparency (5.30% cap, trajectory, peak, gap), and the Bank Rate pause the paper couldn't have anticipated (foreword closed 23 December 2025 with 'markets expect bank rates to be next cut in April 2026'; Bank Rate is still 3.75% at 16 August). officer.body:
Hi Jon,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO curve, and a training academy for officers and members. More — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep the data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since a strategy was set. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy and Capital Strategy that went to Full Council on 20 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The paper is unusually candid on the trade-offs, and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The Welsh Government MRP payment-holiday flexibility for 2026-27 is folded into your MRP policy to give you the discretion, and the cover paper says outright in the same paragraph that it is difficult to see how this new flexibility complies with the Wellbeing of Future Generations Act. Of the councils we've read this year that both take the discretion in case it's needed AND publish an equivalent reservation on the record, there aren't many. The distinction between contingency and intention — you also state plainly that there are no plans to use it to bridge the projected funding gap and balance the 2026-27 budget — sits in the same paragraph. Most of the sector treats the new flexibility, where it addresses it at all, as a technical option; framing it as a Future Generations question is a different move.

The generational framing is repeated on page 4 of the Capital Strategy — the sentence asking whether future generations of Pembrokeshire should be paying for borrowing incurred now, with the £60k-a-year-per-£1m-at-4.0% arithmetic underneath. That is what the 5.30% General Fund cap methodology, approved by Council in December 2023, is built on. Table 1 on page 29 has the approved programme sitting at 3.92% in 2026-27 then 4.15%, 4.13%, 4.01%, with 1.15% to 1.38% of capacity from 2026-27 through 2029-30. Table 2 then models the additional £149m required to 2041-42 and the outer-year ratio comes out at 5.29% — one basis point under the cap. And you then set the £299m schemes-on-horizon total (Table 3) against the £129.7m of capacity left, so the £169m gap is on the same page as the constraint that produces it. Most papers print one of those four numbers; you've printed all four in the same document.

The market has stalled where the foreword left it. The economic background closes on 23 December, days after the Bank Rate cut to 3.75%, and the paper flagged the markets expecting the next cut in April 2026. Eight months on Bank Rate is still 3.75% — no further cut has come. The £60k-per-£1m at 4.0% assumption still frames things soundly, but the pause is worth having live given Table 4 has £84.8m of loan financing profiled in 2026-27, more than double the £47.4m for 2025-26. We publish the daily fixings at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard and the monthly sector activity — how much local authorities actually borrowed, at what maturity, at what rate — at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. Watching sector activity ahead of a decision to draw is more useful than after.

The liability benchmark pathway on the platform is worth a look too. It's interactive and live, and with CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates it becomes central for everyone — the interactive version lets you stress the Table 2 pressures directly against the 5.30% cap.

On training, four fit this paper. "Cost of carry and internal borrowing" picks up the slippage-benefit paragraph on page 28 — using cashflow and short-term borrowing to limit expensive long-term debt is exactly what that course covers. "MRP policy in practice" sits directly on the payment-holiday discretion. "Strategic PWLB borrowing" is written for the profile of loan financing you have in 2026-27. "Members' introduction to treasury" is written for the annual strategy cycle. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.
